questions.question: What is the two-pointer technique, and when can you use it?
questions.title: Two pointers and the invariant between them
questions.direct_answer: The two-pointer technique tracks two positions and moves one or both according to a rule. It is especially useful for sorted arrays, opposite-end comparisons, in-place compaction, and contiguous ranges where pointer movement safely removes impossible choices.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Each pointer has a clear meaning.
Movement must discard only impossible choices.
Sorted input often enables opposite-end pointers.
Same-direction pointers support windows and compaction.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Two pointers means keeping two indices instead of restarting a nested scan. They may begin at opposite ends or move in the same direction. The important part is an invariant that explains why moving one pointer cannot lose a valid answer.

For example, in a sorted array, if the left and right values sum below a target, moving the left pointer right is safe because keeping the smaller value with any earlier right position cannot produce a larger sum. A palindrome check instead moves both ends inward after comparing them.

This often turns O(n²) pair work into O(n), but it is not automatic. The input order or problem rule must justify each move. If sorting is required first, include its O(n log n) cost and decide whether changing the original order is allowed.

sections.title: Pointer movement needs a proof
sections.content:
An invariant states what remains true before and after every move. For example, in a sorted target-sum search, all pairs outside the current `[left, right]` range have already been ruled out. That statement is why one comparison can eliminate a group of pairs.

Same-direction pointers have a different meaning. A read pointer inspects every value while a write pointer marks the next valid output position, or a left boundary follows a right boundary to maintain a valid window.

sections.title: Common pointer layouts
sections.content:
| Layout | Typical problem | Movement |
|---|---|---|
| Opposite ends | Palindrome or sorted pair | Move one or both inward |
| Read and write | In-place compaction | Read every item; write valid items |
| Sliding window | Contiguous range | Expand right; shrink left by a condition |

questions.question: How do you check whether a string is a palindrome with two pointers?
questions.title: Palindrome check from both ends
questions.direct_answer: Place one pointer at each end, compare the characters, and move inward while they match. Return false on the first mismatch and true when the pointers meet or cross.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Start at the left and right ends.
A mismatch ends the check immediately.
Move both pointers after a match.
Clarify whether case and punctuation are ignored.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. Two pointers compare the mirror positions directly: one begins at index zero and the other at the last index, and both move toward the centre after every match.

For example, `level` compares `l` with `l`, then `e` with `e`, and stops successfully at the middle `v`. `lever` fails on the first comparison because `l` and `r` differ.

The exact-string version is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. A phrase problem such as `A man, a plan, a canal: Panama` needs a stated rule for skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing case. Complex Unicode text may require normalization and grapheme-aware comparison beyond simple string indices.

sections.title: Mirror positions define the invariant
sections.content:
Before each iteration, every character outside the pointer range has already matched its mirror. A mismatch inside proves the whole string is not a palindrome; crossing the pointers proves every required pair matched.

Creating a cleaned reversed string is also valid but uses extra memory. The pointer version is valuable when the requirement asks for constant auxiliary space or when ignored characters can be skipped in place.

questions.question: How do you find a pair with a target sum in a sorted array?
questions.title: Target sum in a sorted array
questions.direct_answer: Compare the values at the two ends. Move the left pointer right when the sum is too small, move the right pointer left when it is too large, and return the pair when the sum matches the target.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The array must be sorted for this movement rule.
Too small means increase the left value.
Too large means decrease the right value.
Return indices or values according to the contract.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
For a sorted array, opposite-end pointers can find a target pair in one pass. The left pointer holds the smallest remaining value and the right pointer holds the largest remaining value.

For example, in `[1, 2, 4, 6, 10]` with target `8`, `1 + 10` is too large, so the right pointer moves left. `1 + 6` is too small, so the left pointer moves right. `2 + 6` matches, giving the pair.

The search is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. It depends on sorted order; sorting an unsorted input first costs O(n log n) and changes original index positions unless pairs carry their indices. The answer contract should also say whether one pair, all pairs, or unique value pairs are required.

sections.title: Sorted order eliminates ranges of pairs
sections.content:
When a sum is too small, pairing the current smallest value with any value no larger than the current right cannot help, so the left value can be discarded. The symmetric argument moves the right pointer after a sum that is too large.

A hash map solves the unsorted one-pair version in O(n) average time with O(n) space. Two pointers trade that extra lookup space for the stronger sorted-input condition.

sections.title: Sorted pair search

questions.question: How do you remove duplicates from a sorted array in place?
questions.title: In-place sorted-array compaction
questions.direct_answer: Keep a write pointer for the last unique value and scan with a read pointer. When the read value differs, advance the write pointer and copy it there; return the new logical length.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Sorted duplicates are adjacent.
Read inspects every value.
Write marks the unique prefix.
Only the returned prefix is part of the result.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Because the array is sorted, equal values appear next to each other. A read pointer scans every element, while a write pointer marks the end of the unique prefix already built in the same array.

For example, `[1, 1, 2, 2, 3]` begins with write at index zero. The read pointer skips repeated `1`, copies `2` to index one, skips the next `2`, and copies `3` to index two. The function returns length `3`, and the valid prefix is `[1, 2, 3]`.

The method is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Values after the returned length are unspecified old storage and should be ignored. The adjacent-duplicate rule depends on sorting; an unsorted array needs a Set, sorting, or a different requirement about order.

sections.title: The unique-prefix invariant
sections.content:
At every step, indices zero through write contain each distinct value seen so far exactly once. Comparing the read value with `values[write]` decides whether it extends that prefix.

In-place interview problems often return a logical length because a JavaScript array is still physically the same size. Truncating `values.length = newLength` is optional and changes the container beyond the classic contract.

sections.title: Compact a sorted array

questions.question: How do you move all zeros to the end of an array in place?
questions.title: Stable in-place zero movement
questions.direct_answer: Use a write pointer for the next non-zero position. Scan once, swap each non-zero value into that position, and advance write; the non-zero values keep their original relative order.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Read scans every element once.
Write marks the next non-zero slot.
Swap only when read and write differ.
Compare with zero, not general falsiness.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A stable in-place solution uses a read pointer to inspect every value and a write pointer for the next position that should contain a non-zero value. When read finds a non-zero value, it swaps that value with the write position and advances write.

For example, `[0, 1, 0, 3, 12]` moves `1` to index zero, `3` to index one, and `12` to index two, producing `[1, 3, 12, 0, 0]`. The non-zero values remain in their original order.

The method is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The condition must be `value !== 0`; using truthiness would also treat `false`, an empty string, or `NaN` as a zero-like value. If mutation is not allowed, return a new array and state the O(n) space cost.

sections.title: The compacted-prefix invariant
sections.content:
Before each read step, every position before write contains the non-zero values seen so far in their original order. The area from write to read contains zeros or values not yet placed.

A two-pass version can first overwrite the prefix with non-zero values and then fill the remainder with zeros. Swapping completes the same work in one pass and avoids overwriting a value before it is inspected.

sections.title: Stable zero movement
